prompt: Which statement about Bubble Sort is correct?
options: Random pivot selection gives Bubble Sort a Θ(n) best case.
An early-exit flag that stops when a full pass makes zero swaps gives Bubble Sort a Θ(n) best case.
Using a temporary array gives Bubble Sort a Θ(n) best case.
Bubble Sort has a Θ(n) best case even without any optimization.
explanation: If a complete pass performs no swap, the array is provably sorted and the algorithm may stop — that single pass costs Θ(n). Without the flag the naive version still runs all n−1 passes, giving Θ(n²) even on sorted input. Bubble Sort has no pivot and needs no temp array.

prompt: Bubble Sort — which two statements are correct?
options: After the i-th pass, the i largest elements are guaranteed to be in their final positions at the end of the array.
Bubble Sort is stable, because it only ever swaps strictly out-of-order adjacent pairs.
Bubble Sort's worst case is Θ(n log n) on reverse-sorted input.
Bubble Sort needs Θ(n) additional memory for the swap buffer.
explanation: Each pass bubbles the largest remaining element to the end, so after i passes the last i slots are final ✓. Only `A[j] > A[j+1]` triggers a swap, so equal elements never cross ⟹ stable ✓. The worst case is Θ(n²) ✗, and swapping needs only Θ(1) extra space ✗.

prompt: Bubble Sort compared with Insertion Sort — which two statements are correct?
options: Both have Θ(n²) average and worst case, and both are stable and in place.
Insertion Sort is usually faster in practice because it performs fewer actual operations per element.
Bubble Sort is asymptotically faster than Insertion Sort in the average case.
Only Insertion Sort can achieve a Θ(n) best case; Bubble Sort cannot, even when optimized.
explanation: They share the same asymptotic profile and both are stable in-place comparison sorts ✓, but Insertion Sort shifts rather than repeatedly swapping, so its constants are smaller ✓. Neither is asymptotically faster than the other ✗, and optimized Bubble Sort *does* reach Θ(n) on sorted input ✗.
